name: Default Curriculum
description: The comprehensive learning path from absolute beginner to full-stack developer, aligned with the Edmonds College CIS Web Application Developer Certificate.

exercises.title: Your First HTML Page
exercises.description: Create a basic HTML page with the required document structure.
exercises.instructions:
Every HTML page needs a basic structure to work properly. Create a valid HTML5 page by adding the required elements.

Your page should have:
- A `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration at the very top
- An `<html>` element with `lang="en"`
- A `<head>` section
- A `<body>` section

This is the skeleton that every web page is built on.
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Add the DOCTYPE declaration -->

<!-- Add the html element with lang="en" -->

  <!-- Add the head section -->

  <!-- Add the body section -->
exercises.solution:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
hints: Every HTML page starts with a special declaration that tells the browser what version of HTML you are using. What does that declaration look like?
The structure is: DOCTYPE at the top, then an <html> element that contains both a <head> and a <body> section.

exercises.title: Page Title
exercises.description: Add a title to your HTML page that appears in the browser tab.
exercises.instructions:
The `<title>` element sets the text that appears in the browser tab. It must be placed inside the `<head>` section.

Add a `<title>` element inside the `<head>` with the text "My First Page".

Example: When you open a website, the text you see on the browser tab is the page title.
exercises.starterCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <!-- Add a title element with the text "My First Page" -->

  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
exercises.solution:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>My First Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
hints: There is a specific HTML element that controls what text appears in the browser tab. Where should it be placed — in the head or the body?
The <title> element goes inside the <head> section. The text you want displayed goes between the opening and closing title tags.

resources.label: W3Schools: HTML Head
resources.description: What goes in the HTML head section

exercises.title: Head and Body
exercises.description: Add a title in the head and a heading in the body of an HTML page.
exercises.instructions:
The `<head>` contains information about the page (like the title). The `<body>` contains what visitors actually see.

Add:
- A `<title>` element inside `<head>` with the text "Hello World"
- An `<h1>` element inside `<body>` with the text "Welcome!"

Remember: The head is for the browser, the body is for the viewer.
exercises.starterCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <!-- Add a title with "Hello World" -->

  </head>
  <body>
    <!-- Add an h1 heading with "Welcome!" -->

  </body>
</html>
exercises.solution: Welcome!
hints: The page has two main sections. One holds information the browser uses behind the scenes, and the other holds content the visitor sees on screen.
Use <title> inside <head> for the tab text. Use <h1> inside <body> for the visible heading.

exercises.title: Heading Levels
exercises.description: Use heading elements h1 through h3 to create a content hierarchy.
exercises.instructions:
HTML has six levels of headings, from `<h1>` (most important) to `<h6>` (least important). They create a visual and structural hierarchy for your content.

Add the following headings in order:
- An `<h1>` with "Main Title"
- An `<h2>` with "Section Title"
- An `<h3>` with "Subsection Title"

Every page should have exactly one `<h1>`. Use `<h2>` through `<h6>` for subsections.

<!-- Add an h1 heading with "Main Title" -->

<!-- Add an h2 heading with "Section Title" -->

<!-- Add an h3 heading with "Subsection Title" -->
exercises.solution:
Main Title

Section Title

Subsection Title
hints: HTML provides numbered heading elements for different levels of importance. The number indicates the level in the hierarchy.
Use <h1> for the most important heading, <h2> for the next level, and <h3> for the level after that. Each has an opening and closing tag.

exercises.title: Bold and Italic
exercises.description: Use strong and em elements to add emphasis to text.
exercises.instructions:
HTML provides elements to add emphasis to text:
- `<strong>` makes text **bold** — use it for important content
- `<em>` makes text *italic* — use it for stressed emphasis

Create a paragraph that contains:
- The word "important" wrapped in `<strong>` tags
- The word "really" wrapped in `<em>` tags

The full text should read: "This is really important information."
exercises.starterCode: This is information.
exercises.solution: This is really important information.
hints: There are two HTML elements that change how text looks and what it means to screen readers. One makes text bold, the other italic.
Wrap the word in the appropriate tag: word for bold, word for italic. These go inside the paragraph.

exercises.description: Use the br element to create line breaks within a paragraph.
exercises.instructions:
In HTML, pressing Enter in your code does NOT create a new line on the page. To force a line break without starting a new paragraph, use the `

hints: HTML ignores extra whitespace and line breaks in your code. There is a special element that forces the browser to move to the next line.

The
element creates a line break. It does not need a closing tag. Place it after each line of text where you want a break.

exercises.title: Preformatted Text
exercises.description: Use pre and code elements to display code snippets on a page.
exercises.instructions:
The `
` element preserves whitespace and line breaks exactly as you type them. The `` element marks text as computer code and displays it in a monospace font.

Create:
- A `
` that says "Here is a code example:"
- A `
` element containing a `` element with the text: `let name = "Alex";`

The `

exercises.title: Unordered List
exercises.description: Create a bulleted list using ul and li elements.
exercises.instructions:
An unordered list displays items with bullet points. It uses two elements:
- `<ul>` — the list container (unordered list)
- `<li>` — each item in the list (list item)

Create an unordered list with three items:
- "Apples"
- "Bananas"
- "Oranges"

Every `<li>` must be inside a `<ul>` to work correctly.
exercises.solution:
• Apples
  • Bananas
  • Oranges
hints: An unordered list needs a container element and individual item elements inside it. What are the HTML tags for these?
The container is <ul> (unordered list). Each item uses <li> (list item) with the text between opening and closing tags.

exercises.title: Ordered List
exercises.description: Create a numbered list using ol and li elements.
exercises.instructions:
An ordered list displays items with numbers. It uses `<ol>` instead of `<ul>`, but the items still use `<li>`.

Create an ordered list with three steps:
1. "Preheat the oven"
2. "Mix the ingredients"
3. "Bake for 30 minutes"

The browser automatically numbers each item for you.
exercises.solution:
1. Preheat the oven
  2. Mix the ingredients
  3. Bake for 30 minutes
hints: A numbered list works just like a bulleted list, but uses a different container element. What tag creates a numbered (ordered) list?
Change <ul> to <ol> for ordered lists. The <li> elements stay the same — the browser handles the numbering automatically.

exercises.title: Grocery List
exercises.description: Build a grocery list with a heading and an unordered list of items.
exercises.instructions:
Practice combining elements by building a grocery list page.

Create:
- An `<h2>` with "Grocery List"
- A `<ul>` with at least 5 items of your choice

Example items: Milk, Bread, Eggs, Butter, Cheese

This combines what you have learned about headings and lists.
exercises.solution:
Grocery List

  • Milk
  • Bread
  • Eggs
  • Butter
  • Cheese

testCases.description: At least 5 <li> elements in the list

hints: You need two types of elements: one for the title of the list and one for the list itself with individual items inside.
Use <h2> for the heading. Then create a <ul> with five or more <li> elements, each containing a grocery item.

exercises.title: External Link
exercises.description: Create a link to an external website using the anchor element.
exercises.instructions: Links are created with the `` (anchor) element. The `href` attribute tells the browser where the link goes. Create a link that: - Has the text "Visit Example" - Points to "https://example.com" The format is: `Link Text` The text between the tags is what the user clicks on.
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Create a link to https://example.com -->
<!-- The link text should say "Visit Example" -->
exercises.solution: Visit Example
hints: Links use a special element with an attribute that specifies the destination URL. What element creates a clickable link?
The <a> element creates a link. The href attribute sets the destination. Your text goes between the opening and closing tags.

resources.description: How to create links in HTML

exercises.title: Descriptive Link Text
exercises.description: Write links with meaningful text instead of generic phrases.
exercises.instructions:
Good link text describes where the link goes. Screen readers announce link text to users, so "click here" is unhelpful.

Create two links:
- A link to "https://www.w3schools.com" with the text "W3Schools HTML Tutorial"
- A link to "https://developer.mozilla.org" with the text "MDN Web Docs"

Bad: "Click here to learn HTML"
Good: "Learn HTML at W3Schools"
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Create a link to W3Schools with descriptive text -->

<!-- Create a link to MDN with descriptive text -->
exercises.solution: W3Schools HTML Tutorial MDN Web Docs
hints: Each link needs two things: a destination URL and descriptive text. The text should tell the user where the link leads.
Create two <a> elements, each with an href attribute pointing to the correct URL and descriptive text between the tags.

exercises.title: Open in New Tab
exercises.description: Create a link that opens in a new browser tab safely.
exercises.instructions: Sometimes you want a link to open in a new tab so the user does not leave your page. Use the `target` attribute: - `target="_blank"` opens the link in a new tab - `rel="noopener"` should always be added for security when using `_blank` Create a link that: - Points to "https://example.com" - Has the text "Open Example in New Tab" - Opens in a new tab safely Format: `Text`
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Create a link that opens in a new tab -->
<!-- Include target="_blank" and rel="noopener" -->
exercises.solution: Open Example in New Tab
hints: Links have attributes beyond href that control behavior. What attributes make a link open in a new tab?
Add target="_blank" to open in a new tab. Always pair it with rel="noopener" for security. Both go inside the opening <a> tag.

resources.description: Anchor element attributes including target and rel

exercises.title: Email Link
exercises.description: Create a link that opens the user's email program.
exercises.instructions: You can create a link that opens the user's email program by using `mailto:` in the `href` attribute instead of a URL. Create a link that: - Opens an email to "hello@example.com" - Has the text "Send us an email" Format: `Text`
exercises.starterCode: <!-- Create an email link to hello@example.com -->
exercises.solution: Send us an email
hints: Links do not always have to point to web pages. The href attribute supports a special protocol for opening email programs.
Instead of https://, use mailto: followed by the email address in the href attribute.

exercises.description: Add an image to a page using the img element with src and alt attributes.

The element needs src for the file path and alt for the description. It does not need a closing tag.

exercises.title: Image Sizing
exercises.description: Set the width and height of an image using HTML attributes.
exercises.instructions: You can control the size of an image using the `width` and `height` attributes directly on the `` element. Add an image with: - `src` set to "banner.jpg" - `alt` set to "Website banner" - `width` set to "600" - `height` set to "200" The values are in pixels. Setting these attributes helps the browser reserve space for the image while the page loads.
exercises.starterCode: <!-- Add an image with width and height attributes -->
hints: Images can have attributes that control their display size on the page. What attributes set the dimensions of an image?
Add width and height attributes to the tag with numeric values (no units needed — they default to pixels).

exercises.title: Linked Image
exercises.description: Wrap an image inside a link to make it clickable.
exercises.instructions: You can make an image clickable by wrapping it inside an `` element. When the user clicks the image, they follow the link. Create a link to "https://example.com" that contains an image: - Image `src`: "logo.png" - Image `alt`: "Example Logo" Format: ``
exercises.starterCode: <!-- Create a link that contains a clickable image -->
hints: You already know how to create links and how to add images. What happens if you put one element inside the other?
Place the element between the opening and closing tags. The image becomes the clickable content of the link.

exercises.title: Simple Table
exercises.description: Create a basic 2-column table with 3 rows of data.
exercises.instructions:
Tables use three main elements:
- `<table>` — the table container
- `<tr>` — a table row
- `<td>` — a table data cell

Create a table with 3 rows and 2 columns:
- Row 1: "Name" and "Age"
- Row 2: "Alex" and "25"
- Row 3: "Sam" and "30"

Each `<td>` goes inside a `<tr>`, and all `<tr>` elements go inside `<table>`.
exercises.solution:
Name Age
Alex 25
Sam 30

testCases.description: At least 6 <td> cells exist (3 rows × 2 columns)

hints: Tables are built row by row. Each row contains cells. What elements create a table row and a table cell?
Use <tr> for each row and <td> for each cell within that row. Nest them inside a <table> element.

resources.label: W3Schools: HTML Tables
resources.description: How to create tables in HTML

exercises.title: Table Headers
exercises.description: Use th elements to create bold header cells in a table.
exercises.instructions:
The `<th>` element creates a header cell that is bold and centered by default. Use `<th>` instead of `<td>` for the first row to label your columns.

Create a table with:
- A header row using `<th>` with "Product" and "Price"
- Two data rows using `<td>`:
  - "Coffee" and "$3.00"
  - "Tea" and "$2.50"
exercises.starterCode:
Coffee $3.00
Tea $2.50
exercises.solution:
Product Price
Coffee $3.00
Tea $2.50
hints: Header cells use a different element than regular data cells. What element creates a bold, centered header in a table?
Replace <td> with <th> for the first row to create header cells. Data rows still use <td>.

exercises.title: Table Sections
exercises.description: Organize a table into head, body, and foot sections.
exercises.instructions:
Tables can be divided into three sections for better organization:
- `<thead>` — the header section (column labels)
- `<tbody>` — the body section (data rows)
- `<tfoot>` — the footer section (summary row)

Create a table with:
- `<thead>` containing a row with `<th>` cells: "Item" and "Cost"
- `<tbody>` containing two rows: "Lunch" / "$12" and "Dinner" / "$25"
- `<tfoot>` containing a row: "Total" and "$37"
exercises.solution:
Item Cost
Lunch $12
Dinner $25
Total $37
hints: Tables can be split into logical sections. What three elements divide a table into header, body, and footer areas?
Wrap your header row in <thead>, your data rows in <tbody>, and your summary row in <tfoot>. Each section still uses <tr> and <td>/<th> inside.

resources.label: MDN: thead element
resources.description: Table head, body, and foot sections

exercises.title: Text Input
exercises.description: Create a text input with a label using the label and input elements.
exercises.instructions:
Form inputs let users enter data. Every input should have a `<label>` that describes it.

Create:
- A `<label>` with the text "Your Name:" and a `for` attribute set to "name"
- An `<input>` with `type="text"` and `id="name"`

The `for` attribute on the label must match the `id` on the input. This connects them so clicking the label focuses the input.
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Add a label for the input -->

<!-- Add a text input with matching id -->
exercises.solution:
<label for="name">Your Name:</label>
<input type="text" id="name">
hints: Form inputs need a visible description and an interactive element where the user types. What two elements work together for this?
Use <label> with a for attribute and <input> with a matching id attribute. The for and id values must be identical.

resources.label: MDN: input element
resources.description: The input element and its types

exercises.title: Form with Button
exercises.description: Build a simple form with a text input and a submit button.
exercises.instructions:
Forms collect user input. A basic form needs:
- A `<form>` container
- An `<input>` for the user to type in
- A `<button>` to submit the form

Create a form with:
- A text input with `id="email"` and `placeholder="Enter your email"`
- A `<button>` with `type="submit"` and the text "Submit"

  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
hints: A form is a container that groups inputs and a button together. What element wraps all form content?
The <form> element contains your inputs and button. The input uses placeholder for hint text, and the button uses type="submit".

exercises.title: Input Types
exercises.description: Use different input types for email, password, and number fields.
exercises.instructions:
The `<input>` element supports many types. Each type changes the behavior:
- `type="email"` — validates email format
- `type="password"` — hides the text as dots
- `type="number"` — only allows numbers

Create three labeled inputs:
- Label "Email:" with an email input (`id="email"`)
- Label "Password:" with a password input (`id="password"`)
- Label "Age:" with a number input (`id="age"`)

hints: The input element has a type attribute that changes its behavior. What type values create fields for email, hidden text, and numbers?
Set type="email" for email validation, type="password" to hide text, and type="number" to only allow numeric input.

exercises.title: Placeholder Text
exercises.description: Add placeholder text to inputs that shows hint text before the user types.
exercises.instructions:
The `placeholder` attribute displays gray hint text inside an input. It disappears when the user starts typing.

Create a form with two inputs:
- A text input with `placeholder="Enter your full name"`
- An email input with `placeholder="you@example.com"`

Placeholders help users understand what to type.

  <input type="email" <!-- add placeholder -->>
</form>
exercises.solution:
<form>
  <input type="text" placeholder="Enter your full name">
  <input type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">
</form>
hints: There is an input attribute that shows temporary hint text inside the field before the user types anything.
Add placeholder="..." to each input element. The placeholder value is the hint text shown in gray.

exercises.title: Checkboxes and Radio Buttons
exercises.description: Create checkbox and radio button inputs for selections.
exercises.instructions:
Checkboxes let users select multiple options. Radio buttons let users select only one option from a group.

- `type="checkbox"` — can select multiple
- `type="radio"` — can select only one (group them with the same `name`)

Create:
- A checkbox with `id="agree"` and label "I agree to the terms"
- Two radio buttons with `name="color"`: one with `id="red"` labeled "Red", another with `id="blue"` labeled "Blue"

Radio buttons with the same `name` form a group — selecting one deselects the others.
exercises.starterCode:
<!-- Checkbox -->
<input <!-- set type and id -->>
<label for="agree">I agree to the terms</label>

<!-- Radio button group -->
<input <!-- set type, name, and id -->>
<label for="red">Red</label>

<input <!-- set type, name, and id -->>
<label for="blue">Blue</label>
exercises.solution:
<input type="checkbox" id="agree">
<label for="agree">I agree to the terms</label>

<input type="radio" name="color" id="red">
<label for="red">Red</label>

hints: There are two input types for selection: one allows multiple choices, the other allows only one. What input types are these?
Use type="checkbox" for multi-select and type="radio" for single-select. Radio buttons must share the same name attribute to form a group.

exercises.title: Header and Footer
exercises.description: Use header and footer elements to define the top and bottom of a page.
exercises.instructions:
Semantic HTML elements describe the role of content on the page. The `
` and `
` elements mark the top and bottom sections. Create: - A `
` containing an `

` with "My Website" - A `
` containing a `

` with "© 2026 My Website" These elements help browsers and screen readers understand the structure of your page.

My Website

Use <header> for the top section and <footer> for the bottom. Place your heading inside the header and your copyright text inside the footer.

exercises.title: Nav Element
exercises.description: Use the nav element to wrap navigation links on a page.
exercises.instructions:
The `<nav>` element wraps a section of navigation links. It tells browsers and screen readers that these links are the main way to navigate the site.

Create a `<nav>` element containing three links:
- "Home" linking to "index.html"
- "About" linking to "about.html"
- "Contact" linking to "contact.html"

The <nav> element wraps your links. Place your <a> elements inside it.

exercises.description: Use the main element to wrap the primary content of a page.
exercises.instructions:
The `

` containing an `

` with "Blog" - A `
` containing an `

Footer content

The <main> element wraps your primary content. It sits between the header and footer, and each page should have only one.

exercises.title: Inline Style
exercises.description: Change the text color of a heading using a CSS rule.
exercises.instructions:
CSS can be applied to HTML in three ways: inline (using the `style` attribute directly on an element), internal (using a `<style>` block in the HTML head), or external (linking a separate `.css` file). Writing separate CSS rules is the most common and maintainable approach.

Style the `h1` element so its text color is `blue`.

Inline styles look like `<h1 style="color: blue;">`, but separate CSS rules are preferred because they keep your styles organized.
exercises.providedHtml: Hello World
hints: There is a CSS property that controls the color of text inside an element.
The property is called `color` and it accepts named values like the English word for the color you want.

resources.label: W3Schools: CSS How To
resources.description: Three ways to apply CSS to HTML

exercises.title: Internal Stylesheet
exercises.description: Write CSS rules to style a heading and paragraph with different colors.
exercises.instructions:
An internal stylesheet is a `<style>` block placed in the HTML `<head>`. When you write CSS in this editor, it works just like an internal stylesheet — your rules apply to the HTML on the page.

Style the page so that:
- The `h1` text color is `darkblue`
- The `p` text color is `gray`
exercises.providedHtml:
Welcome

This is a paragraph.
hints: You already know the property that changes text color. Apply it to each element with the color name specified in the instructions.
Use the `color` property inside each rule. Named colors like `darkblue` and `gray` work directly as values.

exercises.title: External Stylesheet
exercises.description: Write CSS rules as they would appear in an external stylesheet file.
exercises.instructions:
An external stylesheet is a separate `.css` file linked to HTML using a `<link>` tag in the `<head>`. The CSS rules you write here work exactly the same way — the only difference is where the file lives.

Write CSS rules to:
- Make all `h1` elements have the color `teal`
- Make all `p` elements have the color `slategray`

External stylesheets are the most common and recommended approach because they keep styles separate from HTML.
exercises.providedHtml:
My Website

External stylesheets keep code organized.
hints: The property and syntax for changing text color is the same whether your CSS is inline, internal, or in an external file.
Use the `color` property with named color values. The syntax is identical regardless of where the CSS file lives.

exercises.title: Style a Heading
exercises.description: Change the size and color of a heading using CSS properties.
exercises.instructions:
CSS properties let you control many aspects of how elements look. Two fundamental properties are `color` (text color) and `font-size` (text size).

Style the `h1` element so that:
- The text color is `crimson`
- The font size is `36px`

This is the foundation of CSS — selecting an element and setting its properties.
exercises.providedHtml: Styled Heading
hints: There are two CSS properties needed — one controls the text color and the other controls how large the text appears.
The `color` property sets text color and `font-size` sets the text size. Use the exact values from the instructions.

exercises.title: Element Selector
exercises.description: Use an element selector to style all paragraphs on a page.
exercises.instructions:
A CSS element selector targets every instance of an HTML element by its tag name. When you write `p { }`, every `

` on the page gets those styles. Style all `p` elements so their text color is `navy`. Element selectors are the simplest type of selector — just use the tag name.
exercises.providedHtml:
First paragraph.

Second paragraph.

Third paragraph.

testCases.description: p elements have navy text color
Last paragraph also has navy text

hints: In CSS, you can target all elements of the same type by writing the tag name as the selector.
Use the tag name `p` as the selector and set the `color` property to the specified color name.

exercises.title: Class Selector
exercises.description: Use a class selector to style elements that share a class name.
exercises.instructions:
A class selector targets elements with a specific `class` attribute. In CSS, class selectors start with a dot (`.`).

The HTML has several elements, some with the class `highlight`. Style all elements with the `highlight` class so their text color is `orangered`.

Classes are reusable — you can apply the same class to many different elements.
exercises.providedHtml:
Important text.

Normal text.

Also important.
hints: Class selectors in CSS start with a special character followed by the class name.
Use a dot (`.`) followed by the class name as your selector. Then set the `color` property inside the rule.

exercises.title: ID Selector
exercises.description: Use an ID selector to style a single element by its unique ID.
exercises.instructions:
An ID selector targets one specific element with a unique `id` attribute. In CSS, ID selectors start with a hash (`#`).

Style the element with the ID `main-title` so its text color is `purple`.

IDs must be unique — only one element per page should have a given ID.
exercises.providedHtml:
Welcome

Subtitle
hints: ID selectors in CSS start with a special character followed by the ID name.
Use a hash (`#`) followed by the ID name as your selector. Then set the `color` property inside the rule.

exercises.title: Multiple Classes
exercises.description: Apply styles to elements using separate class selectors.
exercises.instructions:
Elements can have multiple classes, and you can write separate CSS rules for each class.

The HTML has elements with the classes `bold-text` and `blue-text`. Write CSS rules so that:
- Elements with class `bold-text` have `font-weight` set to `bold`
- Elements with class `blue-text` have `color` set to `steelblue`

An element with both classes will get both styles applied.

Bold paragraph.

Blue paragraph.

Bold and blue.
hints: Each class gets its own CSS rule. The dot before the class name tells CSS it is a class selector.
Write a `.bold-text` rule with `font-weight` and a `.blue-text` rule with `color`. Both rules apply to the third paragraph since it has both classes.

exercises.title: Group Selectors
exercises.description: Style multiple elements at once using a group selector.
exercises.instructions:
A group selector lets you apply the same styles to multiple elements in one rule by separating selectors with commas.

Style `h1`, `h2`, and `h3` elements so they all have the text color `darkslategray`.

Grouping selectors avoids repeating the same CSS rule for each element.

Title

Subtitle

Section

Regular text.
hints: Instead of writing the same style three times, CSS lets you list multiple selectors separated by a specific punctuation mark.
Use commas between selectors to group them. Then set the `color` property inside the shared rule.

exercises.title: Named Colors
exercises.description: Use named CSS colors to style text elements.
exercises.instructions:
CSS supports over 140 named colors like `red`, `blue`, `tomato`, `coral`, and `steelblue`. Named colors are the simplest way to add color to your page.

Style the elements so that:
- The `h1` has text color `tomato`
- The `p` has text color `seagreen`

Named colors are human-readable, but for precise control you will later learn hex, RGB, and HSL values.
exercises.providedHtml:
Colorful Heading

Colorful paragraph.
hints: CSS has a large set of built-in color names that you can use directly as property values.
Use the `color` property with the named color. Color names are just English words — type them exactly as shown.

exercises.title: Hex Colors
exercises.description: Use hexadecimal color codes to set precise text colors.
exercises.instructions:
Hexadecimal (hex) colors start with `#` followed by six characters (0-9 and a-f). Each pair represents red, green, and blue intensity.

Style the elements:
- The `h1` text color should be `#e74c3c` (a red)
- The `p` text color should be `#2c3e50` (a dark blue-gray)

Hex codes give you access to over 16 million colors — far more than named colors.
exercises.providedHtml:
Hex Colors

Precise color control.
hints: Hex color codes start with a `#` symbol followed by six characters that represent red, green, and blue values.

exercises.title: RGB Colors
exercises.description: Use RGB color notation to specify colors with red, green, and blue values.
exercises.instructions:
RGB colors use the `rgb()` function with three numbers from 0 to 255, representing red, green, and blue intensity.

Style the elements:
- The `h1` text color should be `rgb(52, 152, 219)` (a sky blue)
- The `p` text color should be `rgb(155, 89, 182)` (a purple)

RGB is useful when you want to think about colors as a mix of red, green, and blue light.
exercises.providedHtml:
RGB Colors

Mixing light values.
hints: The `rgb()` function takes three numbers separated by commas, each between 0 and 255.
Use `rgb(red, green, blue)` as the value for the `color` property. Copy the exact numbers from the instructions.

exercises.title: Background Color
exercises.description: Set background colors on elements using CSS.
exercises.instructions:
The `background-color` property sets the background color of an element. It works with named colors, hex codes, `rgb()` values, and more.

Style the `.card` element:
- Set `background-color` to `#f0f4f8`
- Set `color` (text) to `#1a202c`

Background colors are essential for creating visual sections and highlighting content.
exercises.providedHtml:
Card Title

Card content goes here.
hints: There is a CSS property specifically for setting the color behind the text and content of an element.
The property is `background-color` (with a hyphen). Set it to the hex value specified in the instructions.

exercises.title: Text and Inheritance
exercises.description: Set text colors and observe how child elements inherit from parents.
exercises.instructions:
The `color` property controls text color and is inherited by child elements. Setting `color` on `body` affects all text on the page unless overridden by a more specific rule.

Style the elements:
- The `body` text color should be `rgb(51, 51, 51)` (a dark gray — easier to read than pure black)
- The `h1` text color should be `rgb(30, 64, 175)` (a rich blue)

The paragraph will inherit the body color automatically. Using dark gray instead of pure black for body text is a common design pattern.
exercises.providedHtml:
Design Tip

Dark gray text is easier to read than pure black on white backgrounds.

testCases.description: p inherits dark gray text color from body

hints: The `color` property on a parent element is inherited by its children, so setting it on `body` affects all text unless overridden.
Set `color` on both `body` and `h1`. The paragraph will automatically inherit the body color since it has no override.

exercises.title: Font Family
exercises.description: Set the font family for text elements with a fallback stack.
exercises.instructions:
The `font-family` property sets which font is used to display text. Always provide fallback fonts in case the first choice is not available.

Style the elements:
- The `body` should use `Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif`
- The `h1` should use `Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif`

The browser tries each font in order and uses the first one available. Always end with a generic family like `sans-serif` or `serif`.
exercises.providedHtml:
Font Families

Different fonts for different purposes.
hints: Fonts are specified as a comma-separated list. If a font name contains spaces, it needs to be wrapped in quotes.
Use `font-family` with a comma-separated list. Generic families like `sans-serif` and `serif` are written without quotes.

exercises.title: Font Size
exercises.description: Control text size using the font-size property with pixel values.
exercises.instructions:
The `font-size` property controls how large text appears. Pixels (`px`) are the simplest unit to start with.

Style the elements:
- The `h1` should have a font size of `32px`
- The `p` should have a font size of `16px`

Font size is one of the most-used CSS properties — it gives you precise control over text readability.

Size Matters

Readable body text is usually between 14px and 18px.
hints: There is a CSS property that controls how large or small text appears on the screen.
The property is `font-size`. Specify the value as a number followed immediately by the unit `px` with no space.

exercises.title: Font Weight
exercises.description: Control text boldness using the font-weight property.
exercises.instructions:
The `font-weight` property controls how thick or thin text characters appear. Common values are `normal` (400), `bold` (700), or numeric values from 100 to 900.

Style the elements:
- The `h1` should have font weight `bold`
- The `.light` paragraph should have font weight `300`

Browsers display headings as bold by default, but you can override this with CSS.
exercises.providedHtml:
Bold Heading

This text is lighter than normal.
hints: There is a CSS property that controls how thick or thin text strokes appear.
The property is `font-weight`. It accepts keywords like `bold` or numeric values like `300`.

exercises.title: Text Alignment
exercises.description: Align text within elements using the text-align property.
exercises.instructions:
The `text-align` property controls the horizontal alignment of text inside an element. Common values are `left`, `center`, `right`, and `justify`.

Style the elements:
- The `h1` should have centered text
- The `.right-aligned` paragraph should have right-aligned text

Text alignment affects all inline content inside the element, including text and inline elements.
exercises.providedHtml:
Centered Title

Default left-aligned text.

Right-aligned text.
hints: There is a CSS property that controls whether text sits to the left, center, or right of its container.
The property is `text-align`. Use it with values like `center` or `right`.

exercises.title: Text Decoration
exercises.description: Add and remove text decorations like underlines and strikethrough.
exercises.instructions:
The `text-decoration` property adds visual decorations to text. Common values include `underline`, `line-through`, `overline`, and `none`.

Style the elements:
- The `.underlined` element should have `text-decoration` set to `underline`
- The `.strikethrough` element should have `text-decoration` set to `line-through`

A common use of `text-decoration: none` is removing the default underline from links.

hints: There is a CSS property that controls lines drawn on, under, or through text.
The property is `text-decoration`. Use `underline` for a line beneath text and `line-through` for a line across text.

exercises.title: Padding
exercises.description: Add inner spacing to an element using the padding property.
exercises.instructions:
The `padding` property adds space between an element's content and its border. It creates breathing room inside the element.

Style the `.box` element:
- Set `padding` to `20px` on all sides

Padding pushes content inward. Think of it like the cushioning inside a picture frame.
exercises.providedHtml: This box needs padding.
hints: There is a CSS property that adds space between an element's content and its edge.
The property is `padding`. A single value like `20px` applies the same spacing to all four sides at once.

exercises.title: Margin
exercises.description: Add outer spacing around an element using the margin property.
exercises.instructions:
The `margin` property adds space outside an element's border, pushing other elements away. It creates distance between elements.

Style the `.box` elements:
- Set `margin` to `16px` on all sides

Margin is the space between elements. Think of it like the gap between picture frames on a wall.
exercises.providedHtml:
First box
Second box
hints: There is a CSS property that adds space outside an element, creating distance from neighboring elements.
The property is `margin`. A single value like `16px` applies the same spacing to all four sides at once.

exercises.title: Border
exercises.description: Add a visible border around an element with color and width.
exercises.instructions:
The `border` shorthand property sets the width, style, and color of an element's border in one line.

Style the `.box` element:
- Add a border that is `2px` wide, `solid` style, and `#3b82f6` color

The border shorthand order is: width style color. The most common border style is `solid`.

Write `border` followed by three values separated by spaces: the width in pixels, the word `solid`, and the color.

exercises.title: Padding Shorthand
exercises.description: Use shorthand notation to set different padding on vertical and horizontal sides.
exercises.instructions:
CSS padding shorthand lets you set different values for each axis in one declaration:
- **2 values:** `padding: vertical horizontal` (top/bottom then left/right)
- **4 values:** `padding: top right bottom left` (clockwise from top)

Style the `.box` element:

Use the 2-value shorthand where the first value is vertical and the second is horizontal.

hints: The padding shorthand can take two values. The first applies to top and bottom, the second to left and right.
Write `padding` followed by two pixel values separated by a space: the vertical padding first, then the horizontal.

exercises.title: Margin Auto
exercises.description: Use margin auto to center a block element horizontally.
exercises.instructions:
The special value `auto` for left and right margins will center a block element horizontally within its parent.

Style the `.centered-box` element:
- Set `width` to `300px`
- Set `margin` to `0` on top and bottom, and `auto` on left and right

Set `width` to a fixed value, then use `margin` with `0` for vertical and `auto` for horizontal.

exercises.title: Border Radius

The `border-radius` property rounds the corners of an element. A single value rounds all four corners equally.

Style the `.box` element:

exercises.title: Pixels
exercises.description: Size elements using pixel units for precise control.
exercises.instructions:
Pixels (`px`) are the most straightforward CSS unit. One pixel is one dot on the screen, giving you exact, predictable sizing.

Style the `.box` element:
- Set `width` to `200px`
- Set `height` to `100px`
- Set `font-size` to `18px`

Pixels are absolute units — they stay the same size regardless of the parent element or browser settings.

Use `width`, `height`, and `font-size` properties, each with a value ending in `px`.

exercises.title: Percentages
exercises.description: Size elements relative to their parent using percentage units.
exercises.instructions:
Percentage units (`%`) size elements relative to their parent. If a parent is `400px` wide, a child with `width: 50%` will be `200px` wide.

Style the elements:
- `.half-width` should have `width` set to `50%`
- `.full-width` should have `width` set to `100%`

Percentages create layouts that adapt to different container sizes.

Half
Full

exercises.title: Em Units

The `em` unit is relative to the font size of the element's parent. If the parent has `font-size: 16px`, then `1.5em` equals `24px` (16 times 1.5).

Style the elements:
- `.container` should have `font-size` set to `16px`
- `.large-text` should have `font-size` set to `1.5em`

Em units create proportional sizing that scales with the base font size.

`, `

`) take up the full width of their parent and stack vertically by default. Style the `.box` elements: - Set `background-color` to `#bfdbfe` - Set `padding` to `12px` - Set `margin-bottom` to `8px` You do not need to set `display: block` because `

exercises.title: Inline Elements

Inline elements (like `<span>`, `<a>`, `<strong>`) flow within text and only take up as much width as their content. Unlike block elements, `width` and `height` have no effect on inline elements.

Setting `display: none` completely removes an element from the page layout. The element is still in the HTML, but it takes up no space and is invisible.

Style the `.hidden` element:

This is commonly used to hide and show elements with JavaScript, or to hide content on certain screen sizes.

exercises.title: Source Order
exercises.description: Understand which CSS rule wins when selectors have equal specificity.

When two CSS rules have the same specificity (selector strength), the rule that appears **last** in the source code wins. This is called the cascade.

The CSS below has two conflicting rules for `p` that set different colors. Add the correct property in the third rule to make the paragraph text `green`.

This demonstrates that source order matters — later rules override earlier ones when specificity is tied.

exercises.title: Declare with Var
exercises.description: Declare three variables using the legacy var keyword.
exercises.instructions:
The `var` keyword is the original way to declare variables in JavaScript. You will see it in older code. Modern JavaScript uses `let` and `const` instead.

Declare three variables using `var`:
1. `username` = `"admin"`
2. `loginCount` = `42`
3. `isActive` = `true`

Example: `var greeting = "hi";`
hints: The `var` keyword works just like `let` for basic declarations — keyword, name, equals sign, value.
Write `var username = "admin";` and follow the same pattern for each variable.

exercises.title: Declare with Const
exercises.description: Declare five constants using the const keyword.
exercises.instructions:
The `const` keyword creates a variable that cannot be reassigned. By convention, true constants use SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE.

Declare these five constants:
1. `MAX_SCORE` = `100`
2. `APP_NAME` = `"CodeForge"`
3. `IS_PRODUCTION` = `false`
4. `PI` = `3.14159`
5. `SPEED_OF_LIGHT` = `299792458`

Example: `const TAX_RATE = 0.08;`
hints: Constants use `const` instead of `let`. The naming convention for true constants is ALL_CAPS_WITH_UNDERSCORES.
Write `const MAX_SCORE = 100;` — strings need quotes, numbers and booleans do not.

exercises.title: Relative Positioning
exercises.description: Nudge an element from its normal position using position relative.
exercises.instructions:
The `position: relative` property lets you move an element from where it would normally appear. Use `top`, `right`, `bottom`, or `left` to offset it.

Style the `.nudged` element:
- Set `position` to `relative`
- Set `top` to `20px` (pushes it down 20px from its normal position)
- Set `left` to `10px` (pushes it right 10px from its normal position)

The element still takes up its original space in the layout — it just renders shifted.
exercises.providedHtml:
Normal paragraph above.

I am nudged.

Normal paragraph below.
hints: There is a position value that shifts an element visually without removing it from the normal document flow.
Set `position: relative` first, then use `top` and `left` to specify how far to shift. Positive `top` moves down, positive `left` moves right.

exercises.title: Absolute Positioning
exercises.description: Position an element precisely within a relative parent.
exercises.instructions:
An element with `position: absolute` is removed from the normal flow and positioned relative to its nearest positioned ancestor (a parent with `position: relative`).

The HTML has a `.container` (already set to `position: relative`) and a `.badge` inside it.

Style the `.badge` element:
- Set `position` to `absolute`
- Set `top` to `0`
- Set `right` to `0`

This pins the badge to the top-right corner of the container.
exercises.providedHtml:
Card content

New
hints: There is a position value that removes an element from the normal flow and positions it relative to its nearest positioned ancestor.
Set `position: absolute`, then use `top: 0` and `right: 0` to pin it to the parent's top-right corner.

exercises.title: Fixed Header
exercises.description: Create a header that stays fixed at the top of the viewport.
exercises.instructions:
An element with `position: fixed` stays in the same position on screen even when the user scrolls. This is commonly used for navigation bars.

Style the `.header` element:
- Set `position` to `fixed`
- Set `top` to `0`
- Set `left` to `0`
- Set `width` to `100%`
- Set `background-color` to `#1e293b`
- Set `color` to `white`

Fixed elements are removed from the document flow, so content may appear behind them.
exercises.providedHtml:
Fixed Navigation

Page content scrolls under the header.
hints: There is a position value that locks an element to a specific spot on the screen, regardless of scrolling.
Set `position: fixed` with `top: 0` and `left: 0` to pin it to the top-left. Add `width: 100%` to span the full viewport.

exercises.title: Enable Flexbox
exercises.description: Apply display flex to a container to enable flexbox layout.
exercises.instructions:
Flexbox is a layout system that arranges items in a row or column. To use it, set `display: flex` on the container element.

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`

Once flexbox is enabled, its children automatically arrange in a horizontal row. Without flexbox, block elements stack vertically.
exercises.providedHtml:
Item 1
Item 2
Item 3
hints: There is a `display` value that activates a powerful one-dimensional layout system on a container.
Set `display: flex` on the container. Its children will immediately arrange in a horizontal row.

exercises.title: Flex Direction
exercises.description: Arrange flex items in a row or column using flex-direction.
exercises.instructions:
The `flex-direction` property controls whether flex items arrange horizontally (`row`) or vertically (`column`).

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`
- Set `flex-direction` to `column`

The default direction is `row` (horizontal). Changing to `column` stacks items vertically, like a list.
exercises.providedHtml:
Top
Middle
Bottom
hints: Flexbox has a property that controls the main axis — whether items lay out left-to-right or top-to-bottom.
Set `flex-direction: column` to stack items vertically. The default is `row` which arranges them horizontally.

exercises.title: Justify Content
exercises.description: Distribute flex items along the main axis using justify-content.
exercises.instructions:
The `justify-content` property controls how items are distributed along the main axis (horizontally in a row, vertically in a column).

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`
- Set `justify-content` to `space-between`

Common values: `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `center`, `space-between`, `space-around`, `space-evenly`.

`space-between` puts equal space between items, with the first and last items flush against the edges.
exercises.providedHtml:
Left
Center
Right
hints: There is a flexbox property that controls how extra space is distributed between and around items along the main axis.
The property is `justify-content`. The value `space-between` pushes the first item to the start and the last to the end, with equal gaps between.

exercises.title: Align Items
exercises.description: Align flex items along the cross axis using align-items.
exercises.instructions:
The `align-items` property controls how items are aligned along the cross axis (vertical in a row, horizontal in a column).

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`
- Set `align-items` to `center`
- Set `height` to `150px` (so there is space to see the vertical alignment)

Common values: `stretch` (default), `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `center`, `baseline`.
exercises.providedHtml:
Short
Taller
Short
hints: There is a flexbox property that controls alignment on the cross axis — perpendicular to the main direction.
The property is `align-items`. Set it to `center` to vertically center items when flex-direction is row.

exercises.title: Gap
exercises.description: Add space between flex items using the gap property.
exercises.instructions:
The `gap` property adds space between flex items without needing margins. It only creates space between items, not around the outer edges.

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`
- Set `gap` to `16px`

The `gap` property is cleaner than margins because it does not add extra space before the first item or after the last.
exercises.providedHtml:
One
Two
Three
hints: There is a CSS property that creates space between items in a flex or grid container without using margins.
The property is `gap`. Set it to a pixel value to add uniform spacing between all flex items.

exercises.title: Enable Grid
exercises.description: Apply display grid and define columns to create a grid layout.
exercises.instructions:
CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system. To use it, set `display: grid` on the container and define columns with `grid-template-columns`.

Style the `.grid` element:
- Set `display` to `grid`
- Set `grid-template-columns` to `200px 200px 200px` (three equal columns)

This creates a 3-column grid where each column is exactly 200px wide.
exercises.providedHtml:
1
2
3
4
5
6
hints: There is a `display` value that activates a two-dimensional layout system, allowing you to define rows and columns.
Set `display: grid` then use `grid-template-columns` with three pixel values separated by spaces to create three columns.

exercises.title: Grid Columns
exercises.description: Use grid-template-columns with different widths to create varied columns.
exercises.instructions:
The `grid-template-columns` property accepts different widths for each column.

Style the `.grid` element:
- Set `display` to `grid`
- Set `grid-template-columns` to `100px 200px 100px` (narrow, wide, narrow)
- Set `gap` to `8px`

This creates a layout with a wider center column — useful for content with sidebars.
exercises.providedHtml:
Sidebar
Main Content
Aside
hints: Each value in `grid-template-columns` defines the width of one column. Different values create different-sized columns.
List three pixel values separated by spaces: `100px 200px 100px`. Add `gap` for spacing between grid cells.

exercises.title: Grid Rows
exercises.description: Define explicit row heights in a CSS Grid layout.
exercises.instructions:
The `grid-template-rows` property defines the height of each row in the grid.

Style the `.grid` element:
- Set `display` to `grid`
- Set `grid-template-columns` to `1fr 1fr` (two equal-width columns)
- Set `grid-template-rows` to `80px 120px` (first row shorter, second taller)
- Set `gap` to `8px`

The `fr` unit means "fraction of available space."
exercises.providedHtml:
Row 1, Col 1
Row 1, Col 2
Row 2, Col 1
Row 2, Col 2
hints: Just like columns, rows can have explicit heights defined with a grid template property.
Use `grid-template-rows` with pixel values for each row. Use `grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr` for two equal columns.

exercises.title: Viewport Meta
exercises.description: Add the viewport meta tag to make a page mobile-friendly.
exercises.instructions:
Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render pages at a desktop width and then zoom out, making text tiny. The viewport meta tag tells the browser to match the device width.

Add a `<meta>` tag inside `<head>` with:
- `name` set to `"viewport"`
- `content` set to `"width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"`

This single tag is the foundation of responsive web design. Every modern web page should include it.
exercises.starterCode:
Mobile-Friendly Page

This page scales correctly on all devices.
exercises.solution:
Mobile-Friendly Page

This page scales correctly on all devices.
hints: There is a special HTML meta tag that tells mobile browsers how to set the page width.
Add a `<meta>` element with `name="viewport"` and a `content` attribute that specifies the width and initial scale.

exercises.title: Fluid Widths
exercises.description: Use percentages and max-width for fluid, responsive sizing.
exercises.instructions:
Fixed pixel widths break on smaller screens. Using percentages with `max-width` creates fluid layouts that adapt to any screen size.

Style the `.content` element:
- Set `width` to `100%`
- Set `max-width` to `600px`
- Set `margin` to `0 auto` (to center it)

This pattern creates a container that shrinks on small screens but never grows wider than 600px on large screens.
exercises.providedHtml:
Responsive Content

This container adapts to the viewport width, up to a maximum.
hints: Combining `width: 100%` with `max-width` creates a container that is fluid but has an upper size limit.
Set `width: 100%` so it fills small screens, `max-width: 600px` to cap the width, and `margin: 0 auto` to center it.

exercises.title: Define a Custom Property
exercises.description: Create a CSS custom property on the root element.
exercises.instructions:
CSS custom properties (also called CSS variables) let you store values and reuse them throughout your stylesheet. They always start with two dashes (`--`).

Define a custom property on `:root`:
- `--primary-color` with the value `#3b82f6`

Then style the `.box` element:
- Set `background-color` to use the custom property with `var(--primary-color)`

The `:root` selector targets the document root, making the variable available everywhere.
exercises.providedHtml: Styled with a CSS variable.

testCases.description: Uses var() to reference the custom property

hints: Custom properties are defined with two dashes at the start of the name and are declared inside a rule block.
Define the variable inside `:root { --primary-color: #3b82f6; }` then reference it with `var(--primary-color)`.

exercises.title: Use Multiple Variables
exercises.description: Apply multiple CSS custom properties to style an element.
exercises.instructions:
Custom properties shine when you define a set of related values and reuse them across your styles.

Define these custom properties on `:root`:
- `--bg-dark` with value `#1e293b`
- `--text-light` with value `#f1f5f9`

Then style the `.card` element:
- Set `background-color` using `var(--bg-dark)`
- Set `color` using `var(--text-light)`

This pattern is the foundation of CSS theming.
exercises.providedHtml:
Dark Card

Styled with CSS custom properties.
hints: Define multiple custom properties inside the same `:root` block, each on its own line.
Each variable follows the pattern `--name: value;`. Reference them with `var(--name)` as the property value.

exercises.title: Box Shadow
exercises.description: Add a shadow effect to an element using box-shadow.
exercises.instructions:
The `box-shadow` property adds a shadow effect around an element's frame. The values are: `x-offset y-offset blur-radius color`.

Style the `.card` element:
- Add a `box-shadow` of `0 2px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.15)`

This creates a subtle shadow below the card (0px horizontal offset, 2px down, 8px blur, with 15% black).

Shadows add depth and make elements feel like they float above the page.
exercises.providedHtml:
Card Title

This card has a shadow.
hints: There is a CSS property that adds a shadow effect around the outside of an element's box.
The property is `box-shadow` with four values: horizontal offset, vertical offset, blur radius, and color.

exercises.title: Text Shadow
exercises.description: Add a shadow effect to text using text-shadow.
exercises.instructions:
The `text-shadow` property adds a shadow behind text characters. The values are the same as box-shadow: `x-offset y-offset blur-radius color`.

Style the `h1` element:
- Add a `text-shadow` of `2px 2px 4px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.3)`
- Set `color` to `#1e40af`

Text shadows can make headings stand out or create visual depth.
exercises.providedHtml:
Shadow Text

Normal paragraph without shadow.
hints: There is a CSS property similar to `box-shadow` but specifically for adding shadow effects to text.
The property is `text-shadow` with the same offset, blur, and color pattern as box-shadow.

exercises.title: Declare a String
exercises.description: Declare five string variables using different quote styles.
exercises.instructions:
Strings hold text data in JavaScript. You can create strings using double quotes `"`, single quotes `'`, or backticks `` ` ``.

Declare five string variables using `const`:
1. `greeting` = `"Hello, world!"` (double quotes)
2. `language` = `'JavaScript'` (single quotes)
3. `message` = `` `Welcome back` `` (backticks)
4. `empty` = `""` (empty string)
5. `fullName` = `"Jane Doe"`
hints: Strings are text wrapped in quotes. JavaScript accepts double quotes, single quotes, and backticks.
Use `const name = "value";` for each — match the quote style shown for each variable.

exercises.title: Declare a Number
exercises.description: Declare five number variables including integers, decimals, and negatives.
exercises.instructions:
Numbers in JavaScript include integers, decimals, and negatives. Numbers do not use quotes.

Declare five number variables using `const`:
1. `score` = `95`
2. `price` = `19.99`
3. `temperature` = `-5`
4. `zero` = `0`
5. `population` = `7900000000`
hints: Numbers are written without quotes. Decimals use a dot, negatives use a minus sign.
Write `const score = 95;` for integers, `const price = 19.99;` for decimals.

exercises.title: Declare a Boolean
exercises.description: Declare five boolean variables using is/has/can naming conventions.
exercises.instructions:
Booleans represent `true` or `false`. By convention, boolean names start with `is`, `has`, or `can`.

Declare five booleans using `const`:
1. `isOnline` = `true`
2. `hasPermission` = `false`
3. `canEdit` = `true`
4. `isLoggedIn` = `false`
5. `hasCompleted` = `true`
hints: Booleans are `true` or `false` without quotes. Adding quotes makes them strings.
Use `const isOnline = true;` — the keywords `true` and `false` are lowercase.

exercises.title: Declare an Array
exercises.description: Declare four arrays containing different types of data.
exercises.instructions:
Arrays are ordered lists in square brackets `[]`. Items are separated by commas.

Declare four arrays using `const`:
1. `scores` = `[95, 87, 73, 100]`
2. `colors` = `["red", "green", "blue"]`
3. `mixed` = `[42, "hello", true, null]`
4. `empty` = `[]`
hints: Arrays use square brackets with items separated by commas.
Write `const scores = [95, 87, 73, 100];` — strings inside arrays still need quotes.

exercises.title: Declare an Object
exercises.description: Declare four objects with different property types.
exercises.instructions:
Objects store key-value pairs in curly braces `{}`. Each property has a name and value separated by a colon.

Declare four objects using `const`:
1. `student` = `{ name: "Alex", age: 25 }`
2. `dimensions` = `{ width: 100, height: 50 }`
3. `config` = `{ theme: "dark", fontSize: 14, isEnabled: true }`
4. `empty` = `{}`
hints: Objects use curly braces with `key: value` pairs separated by commas.
Write `const student = { name: "Alex", age: 25 };` — keys do not need quotes.

exercises.title: Naming Conventions
exercises.description: Declare ten variables following JavaScript naming conventions.
exercises.instructions:
JavaScript naming conventions:
- `camelCase` for regular variables
- `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for true constants
- `is`/`has`/`can` prefix for booleans

Declare these ten variables:
1. `firstName` = `"Maria"` (const)
2. `itemCount` = `0` (let)
3. `isVisible` = `true` (const)
4. `MAX_RETRIES` = `3` (const)
5. `shoppingCart` = `[]` (let)
6. `userProfile` = `{ name: "Alex", role: "student" }` (const)
7. `currentScore` = `85` (let)
8. `API_BASE_URL` = `"https://api.example.com"` (const)
9. `hasSeenWelcome` = `false` (let)
10. `defaultColor` = `"blue"` (const)
hints: camelCase means lowercase first word, uppercase each following word. True constants use ALL_CAPS.
Use `let` for changing values, `const` for fixed values. Booleans start with is/has/can.

exercises.title: Reassign an Array Element
exercises.description: Change individual elements inside an array using bracket notation.
exercises.instructions:
Arrays are zero-indexed. Change elements with bracket notation: `array[index] = newValue;`

The starter code provides a colors array. Change:
1. `colors[0]` to `"crimson"`
2. `colors[2]` to `"navy"`
3. `colors[4]` to `"violet"`
4. `colors[1]` to `"lime"`
5. `colors[3]` to `"gold"`
hints: Array positions start at 0. The first item is `[0]`, second is `[1]`.
Write `colors[0] = "crimson";` to change the first element.

exercises.title: Reassign an Object Property
exercises.description: Change and add properties on an existing object using dot notation.
exercises.instructions:
Change properties with dot notation: `object.property = newValue;`. Add new properties the same way.

Make these changes to the car object:
1. `car.color` to `"blue"`
2. `car.year` to `2024`
3. `car.model` to `"Corolla"`
4. Add `car.mileage` = `15000`
5. Add `car.isElectric` = `false`
hints: Dot notation: `object.property = value;` to change existing or add new properties.
Write `car.color = "blue";` to change and `car.mileage = 15000;` to add.

exercises.title: Access an Array Element
exercises.description: Extract values from an array using bracket notation and zero-based indexing.
exercises.instructions:
Access elements with bracket notation: `array[index]`. First element is `[0]`.

The starter code provides a planets array. Extract:
1. `first` = `planets[0]`
2. `third` = `planets[2]`
3. `last` = `planets[4]`
4. `secondIndex` = `1`
5. `second` = `planets[secondIndex]`
6. `pair` = `planets[0] + " and " + planets[1]`
7. `totalPlanets` = `5`
hints: Use bracket notation with a number: `planets[0]` gets the first item.
A variable can be used as an index: `planets[secondIndex]` uses the value stored in secondIndex.

exercises.title: Access an Object Property
exercises.description: Extract values from an object using dot notation.
exercises.instructions:
Access properties with dot notation: `object.property`.

Extract from the book object:
1. `bookTitle` = `book.title`
2. `bookAuthor` = `book.author`
3. `publishYear` = `book.year`
4. `pageCount` = `book.pages`
5. `classic` = `book.isClassic`
6. `summary` = `book.title + " by " + book.author`
7. `age` = `2026 - book.year`
hints: Dot notation reads a property: `book.title` returns the value at the `title` key.
Use `+` to join strings: `book.title + " by " + book.author`.

exercises.title: Logical Operator: AND
exercises.description: Evaluate four AND expressions using the && operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `&&` (AND) operator returns `true` only when BOTH sides are `true`.

Using the source variables, evaluate:
1. `result1` = `isLoggedIn && hasPermission` (true && true)
2. `result2` = `isLoggedIn && isAdmin` (true && false)
3. `result3` = `isAdmin && hasPermission` (false && true)
4. `result4` = `isAdmin && isVerified` (false && false)
hints: The `&&` operator needs BOTH values to be `true` to produce `true`. If either side is `false`, the result is `false`.
Write `const result1 = isLoggedIn && hasPermission;` using the variable names from the starter code.

exercises.title: Logical Operator: OR
exercises.description: Evaluate four OR expressions using the || operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `||` (OR) operator returns `true` when at LEAST ONE side is `true`.

Using the source variables, evaluate:
1. `result1` = `isLoggedIn || hasPermission` (true || true)
2. `result2` = `isLoggedIn || isAdmin` (true || false)
3. `result3` = `isAdmin || hasPermission` (false || true)
4. `result4` = `isAdmin || isVerified` (false || false)
hints: The `||` operator only needs ONE side to be `true`. It only returns `false` when both are `false`.
Write `const result1 = isLoggedIn || hasPermission;` using the `||` operator between the two variables.

exercises.title: Logical Operator: NOT
exercises.description: Flip five boolean values using the ! operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `!` (NOT) operator flips a boolean: `true` becomes `false`, `false` becomes `true`.

Flip each value:
1. `result1` = `!isOnline` (flip true)
2. `result2` = `!isBlocked` (flip false)
3. `result3` = `!hasAccess` (flip true)
4. `result4` = `!isMuted` (flip false)
5. `result5` = `!isExpired` (flip true)
hints: The `!` goes directly before the value or variable name, with no space needed.
Write `const result1 = !isOnline;` to flip the boolean value.

exercises.title: Logical Operators: Combined
exercises.description: Evaluate five expressions that combine &&, ||, and ! operators.
exercises.instructions:
Combine logical operators in a single expression. `&&` is evaluated before `||` (like * before + in math).

1. `result1` = `isLoggedIn && hasPermission && isVerified`
2. `result2` = `isAdmin || hasPermission`
3. `result3` = `!isBanned && isLoggedIn`
4. `result4` = `isAdmin && !isBanned || hasPermission`
5. `result5` = `!(isLoggedIn && isAdmin)`
hints: When combining operators, `&&` runs before `||`. Use `!` to flip a single value before combining.
Use the exact variable names from the starter code and combine them with `&&`, `||`, and `!`.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Addition
exercises.description: Evaluate five addition expressions using the + operator.
hints: The `+` operator works with variables and literal numbers. You can add multiple values in one expression.
Write `const sum1 = a + b;` using the variable names provided.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Subtraction
exercises.description: Evaluate five subtraction expressions using the - operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `-` operator subtracts numbers. Results can be negative.

1. `diff1` = `a - b` (20 - 8 = 12)
2. `diff2` = `b - a` (8 - 20 = -12)
3. `diff3` = `c - a` (25 - 20 = 5)
4. `diff4` = `a - 3` (20 - 3 = 17)
5. `diff5` = `c - b - a` (25 - 8 - 20 = -3)
hints: Subtraction can produce negative results when the second number is larger.
Write `const diff1 = a - b;` — subtraction evaluates left to right.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Multiplication
exercises.description: Evaluate five multiplication expressions using the * operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `*` operator multiplies numbers.

1. `total` = `price * quantity` (25 * 4 = 100)
2. `doubled` = `price * 2` (25 * 2 = 50)
3. `tax` = `price * taxRate` (25 * 0.08 = 2)
4. `bulk` = `price * quantity * 2` (200)
5. `discounted` = `price * 0.9` (22.5)
hints: Multiplication uses `*` and works with decimals too. Multiple `*` operations chain together.
Write `const total = price * quantity;` using the variable names provided.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Division
exercises.description: Evaluate five division expressions using the / operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `/` operator divides numbers. Results can be decimals.

1. `perItem` = `total / items` (100 / 4 = 25)
2. `perPerson` = `total / people` (100 / 3 = 33.33...)
3. `half` = `total / 2` (50)
4. `quarter` = `total / 4` (25)
5. `tenth` = `total / 10` (10)
hints: Division uses `/` and can produce decimal results when the numbers do not divide evenly.
Write `const perItem = total / items;` — division evaluates left to right.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Modulo
exercises.description: Evaluate five modulo expressions using the % operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `%` (modulo) operator returns the remainder after division. Useful for checking even/odd.

1. `rem1` = `a % 5` (17 % 5 = 2)
2. `rem2` = `b % 3` (10 % 3 = 1)
3. `rem3` = `c % 2` (8 % 2 = 0, even)
4. `rem4` = `a % 2` (17 % 2 = 1, odd)
5. `rem5` = `a % b` (17 % 10 = 7)
hints: The `%` returns what is left over after dividing. Think: "17 divided by 5 is 3 with remainder 2".
Write `const rem1 = a % 5;` — if the remainder is 0 the number divides evenly.

exercises.title: Math Operators: Combined
exercises.description: Evaluate five expressions following natural operator precedence.
exercises.instructions:
`*` and `/` are evaluated before `+` and `-`, just like in regular math.

1. `result1` = `a + b * c` (10 + 15 = 25)
2. `result2` = `a - b * c` (10 - 15 = -5)
3. `result3` = `a * b + c` (50 + 3 = 53)
4. `result4` = `a / b + c` (2 + 3 = 5)
5. `result5` = `a + b - c * 2` (10 + 5 - 6 = 9)
hints: Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, just like in regular math.
Write the expression exactly as shown — do not add parentheses. Let natural precedence do the work.

exercises.title: Math Operators: Parentheses
exercises.description: Evaluate five expressions where parentheses override natural precedence.
exercises.instructions:
Parentheses `()` force operations inside them to happen first, overriding natural precedence.

1. `result1` = `(a + b) * c` (15 * 3 = 45)
2. `result2` = `a * (b + c)` (10 * 8 = 80)
3. `result3` = `(a - b) * (b - c)` (5 * 2 = 10)
4. `result4` = `a / (b - c)` (10 / 2 = 5)
5. `result5` = `(a + b + c) / 2` (18 / 2 = 9)
hints: Parentheses change the order: `(a + b) * c` adds first, then multiplies.
Write the expressions exactly as shown, with parentheses in the correct places.

exercises.title: Math Operators: Real-World Formulas
exercises.description: Calculate five real-world formulas using math operators and parentheses.
exercises.instructions:
Combine operators and parentheses to solve real-world formulas.

1. `celsius` = `(fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9` (convert 98.6°F)
2. `average` = `(score1 + score2 + score3) / 3`
3. `salePrice` = `originalPrice - (originalPrice * discountPercent / 100)`
4. `totalWithTax` = `subtotal + (subtotal * taxPercent / 100)`
5. `simpleInterest` = `principal * rate * years / 100`
hints: Use parentheses to group the operations that need to happen first, just like in a math formula.
The Celsius formula is `(fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9` — subtract first, then multiply and divide.

exercises.title: Conditional: If
exercises.description: Write five if statements that change a variable when a condition is true.
exercises.instructions:
An `if` statement runs code only when its condition is `true`.

Syntax: `if (condition) { code }`

For each one, a default value is provided. Write an `if` statement that changes it:
1. `weather` starts as `"nice"` → if `temperature > 90`, set to `"hot"`
2. `grade` starts as `"pass"` → if `score < 50`, set to `"fail"`
3. `canDrive` starts as `"no"` → if `age >= 16`, set to `"yes"`
4. `status` starts as `"funded"` → if `balance === 0`, set to `"empty"`
5. `ticket` starts as `"none"` → if `speed > 65`, set to `"speeding"`
hints: An `if` statement checks a condition. If it is true, the code inside the curly braces runs.
Write `if (temperature > 90) { weather = "hot"; }` — the condition goes in parentheses.

exercises.title: Conditional: If Else
exercises.description: Write five if/else statements that choose between two values.
exercises.instructions:
An `if/else` statement chooses between two paths.

Syntax: `if (condition) { A } else { B }`

1. If `hour < 12` → `timeOfDay` = `"morning"`, else `"afternoon"`
2. If `temperature > 60` → `clothing` = `"shorts"`, else `"jacket"`
3. If `score >= 70` → `result` = `"pass"`, else `"fail"`
4. If `balance >= 100` → `canAfford` = `"yes"`, else `"no"`
5. If `age >= 21` → `beverage` = `"coffee or beer"`, else `"coffee"`
hints: `if/else` provides exactly two paths: one for when the condition is true, one for when it is false.
Write `if (hour < 12) { timeOfDay = "morning"; } else { timeOfDay = "afternoon"; }`

exercises.title: Conditional: If Else If Else
exercises.description: Write two multi-branch conditional chains using if/else if/else.
exercises.instructions:
`if/else if/else` chains check multiple conditions in order. The first match wins.

Chain 1 — Letter grade from `score` (82):
- >= 90 → `"A"`, >= 80 → `"B"`, >= 70 → `"C"`, >= 60 → `"D"`, else → `"F"`

Chain 2 — Weather advice from `temp` (45):
- >= 85 → `"Stay hydrated"`, >= 60 → `"Enjoy the weather"`, >= 32 → `"Wear a jacket"`, else → `"Stay inside"`
hints: Start with the highest threshold and work down. The first condition that is true sets the value.
Write `if (score >= 90) { grade = "A"; } else if (score >= 80) { grade = "B"; }` and continue the chain.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Loose Equality
exercises.description: Evaluate six loose equality expressions using the == operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `==` operator checks if values are equal, but converts types first (type coercion). This can cause surprises.

1. `result1` = `num == str` (5 == "5", true — number coerced)
2. `result2` = `zero == emptyStr` (0 == "", true — both falsy)
3. `result3` = `bool == one` (true == 1, true — bool becomes 1)
4. `result4` = `num == 10` (false)
5. `result5` = `zero == false` (0 == false, true)
6. `result6` = `null == undefined` (true — special case)
hints: `==` converts types before comparing. The number 5 and the string "5" are equal with `==` because of coercion.
Write `const result1 = num == str;` — use double equals for each comparison.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Strict Equality
exercises.description: Evaluate seven strict equality expressions using the === operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `===` operator checks both value AND type — no coercion. This is the recommended approach.

1. `result1` = `num === str` (5 === "5", false)
2. `result2` = `num === anotherFive` (5 === 5, true)
3. `result3` = `zero === emptyStr` (0 === "", false)
4. `result4` = `bool === one` (true === 1, false)
5. `result5` = `zero === false` (0 === false, false)
6. `result6` = `num === 5` (true)
7. `result7` = `str === "5"` (true)
hints: `===` requires both the value AND the type to match. The number 5 and string "5" are NOT equal with `===`.
Write `const result1 = num === str;` — use triple equals for each comparison.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Does Not Equal
exercises.description: Evaluate six strict inequality expressions using the !== operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `!==` operator returns `true` when values are NOT equal (or different types).

1. `result1` = `status !== "inactive"` (true)
2. `result2` = `count !== 0` (false)
3. `result3` = `role !== "admin"` (true)
4. `result4` = `score !== 100` (false)
5. `result5` = `theme !== "light"` (true)
6. `result6` = `limit !== 50` (false)
hints: `!==` is the opposite of `===` — it returns true when values are different.
Write `const result1 = status !== "inactive";` — if the values differ, the result is true.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Greater Than / Less Than
exercises.description: Evaluate seven expressions using the > and < operators.
exercises.instructions:
`>` returns true if left is greater. `<` returns true if left is less. Equal values return false for both.

1. `result1` = `age > 17` (true)
2. `result2` = `age < 21` (true)
3. `result3` = `price > 30` (false)
4. `result4` = `temperature < 80` (true)
5. `result5` = `speed > 55` (true)
6. `result6` = `age > 18` (false — equal, not greater)
7. `result7` = `age < 18` (false — equal, not less)
hints: `>` and `<` are strict — equal values return false. To include the boundary, use `>=` or `<=`.
Write `const result1 = age > 17;` — pay attention to the boundary cases with equal values.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Greater or Equal / Less or Equal
exercises.description: Evaluate seven expressions using the >= and <= operators.
exercises.instructions:
`>=` includes the boundary (greater than OR equal). `<=` includes the boundary (less than OR equal).

1. `result1` = `age >= 18` (true, at threshold)
2. `result2` = `age >= 21` (false)
3. `result3` = `balance <= 100` (true, at threshold)
4. `result4` = `balance <= 50` (false)
5. `result5` = `temperature >= 32` (true, at freezing)
6. `result6` = `score <= 100` (true)
7. `result7` = `score >= 70` (true, passing)
hints: `>=` and `<=` include the boundary value — they return true when values are exactly equal.
Write `const result1 = age >= 18;` — the `=` goes AFTER the `>` or `<`.

exercises.title: Comparison Operators: Combined
exercises.description: Evaluate six expressions that combine comparison and logical operators.
exercises.instructions:
Combine comparison (`>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, `===`, `!==`) with logical (`&&`, `||`, `!`) operators.

1. `result1` = `age >= 18 && age <= 65` (working age)
2. `result2` = `score >= 90 || score <= 60` (high or low)
3. `result3` = `balance > 0 && balance < 100`
4. `result4` = `temperature >= 60 && temperature <= 80` (comfortable)
5. `result5` = `hour >= 9 && hour <= 17` (business hours)
6. `result6` = `!(age < 18) && score > 70`
hints: Range checks use `&&` to combine two comparisons: `value >= min && value <= max`.
Write `const result1 = age >= 18 && age <= 65;` — each comparison produces a boolean, then `&&` combines them.

exercises.title: Define a Function
exercises.description: Define a function that returns a greeting string.
exercises.instructions:
A function is a reusable block of code. Use the `function` keyword, give it a name, add parentheses `()`, and curly braces `{}`.

Define a function called `helloWorld` that returns the string `"Hello, World!"`.

Example: `function sayHi() { return "Hi!"; }`
hints: A function needs the `function` keyword, a name, parentheses, and curly braces. Use `return` to send a value back.
The structure is `function helloWorld() { return "Hello, World!"; }`

exercises.title: Define a Function with One Parameter
exercises.description: Define three functions that each accept one parameter.
exercises.instructions:
Parameters let a function receive input. The parameter goes inside the parentheses.

1. `greet(name)` — returns `"Hello, " + name + "!"`
2. `double(number)` — returns `number * 2`
3. `isPositive(number)` — returns `true` if `number > 0`
hints: Parameters are variables listed inside the parentheses. They receive the values passed when the function is called.
